newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economy forecast seen as over-optimistic.
newsitem.headline: Thai economy forecast seen as over-optimistic.

text.p: Thai economic analysts labelled Thursday's central bank economic forecasts for 1996 and 1997 as over-optimistic.

The central bank projected that Thailand's wide current account deficit would narrow next year and that gross domestic product (GDP) growth would rise to 7.1 percent in 1997 from 6.7 percent this year.
Analysts told Reuters the deficit, one of the highest in the region, remained a key worry and that it must show some improvement before they pushed for any Thai investment weighting upgrade.
They said the market would monitor government action to curb the deficit, which the Bank of Thailand said would widen to 8.2 percent of GDP this year but narrow to 7.9 percent next year.

"Even though the c/a deficit is narrowing, it is still considered a big number. We expect that (next year), priorities would be for the cutting of the the deficit," said Paul Alapat, a financial economist at Lehman Brothers.
He added that the 7.1 percent economic growth forecast for next year was too optimistic and said he did not expect to see any recovery until the second half of 1997.

"I'm very sceptical that we can have seven percent plus growth... It is our view that the export slowdown is yet to bottom out," Alapat said. Lehman Brothers has forecast Thailand's 1997 GDP economic growth at six percent.
An area of concern is exports, where the central bank forecast modest growth of 7.7 percent next year from a 0.1 percent contraction seen for this year.
"We don't expect Thai exports to show sustained improvement before the second half of next year," he said.
Another foreign analyst said the current account deficit was "frightening".

"It's pretty frightening when the deficit is this high when the economy has already slowed down sharply... We are nearing the bottom of an economic cycle and yet the gap is still very high," said the analyst who asked not to be named.

He said his company would not upgrade its weighting on Thailand until there were signs of improvement on the current account deficit. "We underweighted Thailand. These figures just continue to confirm our view," he said.

"We want to see an improvement on the current account deficit. We want to see signs that the property bad debt situation improves. We want to see signs that earnings growth is going to return (before upgrading)," he said.

Neil Semple of HG Asia said that the trade deficit seen by the central bank at 474 billion baht in 1997 versus 434 billion this year implied that it expected a big service account surplus of around 60 billion baht.

"The 7.9 percent makes sense if the service account surplus is huge. The market would welcome further comments from the central bank on why the service account surplus would be large next year," Semple said.

Alapat said: "Rather than figures, I think we in the market will focus on political commitments... All this fiscal tightening that has been promised, the slowing down of certain projects. We have to see whether this six-party coalitiion will have the political will to undertake that," he added.
The new government of premier Chavalit Yongchaiyudh has vowed to cut spending and impose strong fiscal discipline.
